extracted.intended_audience: OMB and agency administrative/policy staff evaluating federal employee parking charges (e.g., CIA administrative chiefs, DDA)
extracted.subtask_short: draft OMB employee parking policy review
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate a proposed OMB circular that would charge federal employees for parking, using a cost-benefit approach that accounts for productivity, overtime incentives, energy-conservation goals, and administrative implementability. The memo focuses on agency contexts (e.g., CIA HQ) where the public does not compete for parking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include productivity losses in cost-benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost-benefit analysis of charging federal employees for parking must account for the loss to the government owing to the regularization of work hours — a 'time-clock syndrome' — which naturally follows dependence on strictly scheduled transportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Car-pool and mass-transport users 'almost invariably adhere to a strict eight-hour day and are rarely at work on weekends.' The number of unpaid, professional overtime hours lost can be considerable and should be counted as a cost alongside parking subsidies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether public parking competition exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the general public competes for parking at the facility (e.g., CIA headquarters); if the public does not compete, the usual scarcity rationale for charging employees is weakened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memo notes the omission is 'especially applicable to situations such as at CIA headquarters where the general public does not compete for parking,' implying different justification/metrics are needed when parking is not publicly contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh productivity loss against parking subsidy savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the monetary and non-monetary costs of lost productivity resulting from enforced transit schedules to the savings achieved by reducing parking subsidies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Productivity loss 'is extremely more costly, not only in terms of dollars, but in our case, also in terms of national security.' Thus analyses should quantify both fiscal and mission-related impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain present productivity while supporting energy conservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Any parking policy intended to encourage car pools or mass transit should be designed so as not to undermine overall employee productivity while contributing to the President's energy-conservation program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recommendation explicitly states 'some scheme must be devised for maintaining present productivity without undermining the President's energy-conservation program.' Policy trade-offs must be balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for overtime contribution expectations in policy design
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the parking policy with awareness of existing agency expectations for unpaid overtime (e.g., GS-12 through GS-14 expected to contribute first eight overtime hours weekly; GS-15 and above normally contribute all overtime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because certain grades are expected to donate overtime, charging for parking could effectively penalize those who have voluntarily contributed time; policy should not disincentivize this contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide equitable compensation/credit for uncompensated overtime
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement a scheme to compensate employees who do not receive direct overtime pay by giving credit against parking fees for overtime hours worked (example: $1 per overtime hour up to a monthly maximum equal to the parking fee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a credit would 'defray the monthly cost of parking' and 'provide an incentive for maintaining the productivity of those who have voluntarily donated their time.' The memo gives a concrete illustrative rate and cap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existing compensatory accounting mechanisms where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess administrative feasibility by determining whether existing mechanisms (compensatory overtime accounting) can be used to track and apply overtime credits with little or no added administrative cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memo notes 'a mechanism already exists to maintain an accounting ... under the compensatory category,' suggesting minimal added administrative burden if existing systems are leveraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat equity and administrative cost as part of policy evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Include considerations of equity (fair treatment of employees who donate time) and the expected administrative cost of implementing offsets or incentives as part of the evaluation of charging policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed credit scheme is framed as 'equitable' and administratively inexpensive; analyses should therefore explicitly examine fairness and admin overhead as evaluation dimensions.
